title: End-to-end intelligent voice dispatching driven by a large language model for coal mines
abstract: To address response delays and information errors and omissions caused by reliance on manual call answering and paper records in coal mine dispatching, this study investigated end-to-end intelligent voice dispatching driven by a Large Language Model (LLM) for coal mines. An intelligent voice dispatching system integrating domain fine-tuning with Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) was designed. The system adopted a hierarchically decoupled architecture, used a locally deployed LLM as its decision-making core, and integrated speech recognition and synthesis technologies. By introducing an Interactive Voice Response (IVR) virtual agent mechanism, the system established a closed-loop workflow encompassing call routing, automatic work-order generation, and voice-command execution. Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) fine-tuning was used to adapt the model to the coal mine domain, and RAG was introduced to fundamentally prevent the generation of noncompliant instructions. A vector knowledge base based on the Coal Mine Safety Regulations was constructed as a compliance constraint, enabling end-to-end intelligent processing from voice-command recognition to execution. Field test results showed that, in coal mine environments with high noise levels and strong dialectal accents, the system's speech recognition word error rate was 0.34-0.42. With the semantic compensation capability of the fine-tuned LLM, intent recognition accuracy remained at or above 93.50%, and the average exact match rate of dispatching instructions reached 94.93%. The system operates stably in a mining area and effectively reduces dispatcher workload and the recording error rate, providing a replicable engineering paradigm for intelligent upgrading of coal mines.

title: Brief Announcement: Exponential Quantum Advantage for Message Complexity in Distributed Algorithms
abstract: We investigate how much quantum distributed algorithms can outperform classical distributed algorithms with respect to the message complexity (the overall amount of communication used by the algorithm). Recently, Dufoulon, Magniez and Pandurangan (PODC 2025) have shown a polynomial quantum advantage for several tasks such as leader election and agreement. In this paper, we show an exponential quantum advantage for a fundamental task: routing information between two specified nodes of a network. We prove that for the family of “welded trees” introduced in the seminal work by Childs, Cleve, Deotto, Farhi, Gutmann and Spielman (STOC 2003), there exists a quantum distributed algorithm that transfers messages from the entrance of the graph to the exit with message complexity exponentially smaller than any classical algorithm. Our quantum algorithm is based on the recent “succinct” implementation of quantum walks over the welded trees by Li, Li and Luo (SODA 2024). Our classical lower bound is obtained by “lifting” the lower bound from Childs, Cleve, Deotto, Farhi, Gutmann and Spielman (STOC 2003) from query complexity to message complexity. A full version of this paper can be found on arXiv [21].

title: 9882 Build-a-better-pews? Ai electronic decision support tool to help spot ill children in the paediatric emergency department
abstract: Why did you do this work? The Paediatric Emergency Department is a high-risk environment within which to try and identify unwell children. Paediatric Early Warning Systems (PEWS) help us combine vital physiological observations into an easy to understand score. They are routinely used on inpatient wards and now are being developed for use in the Emergency Department (ED).1 Increasingly, observations are being gathered electronically in the ED, and PEWS automatically calculated rather than scored on paper charts.2 We explored whether machine learning could be used to develop models that could more accurately predict which children are unwell from their observations compared to the current inpatient National PEWS. What did you do? To design a decision support tool specific for the Paediatric ED, we trained machine learning models using extreme gradient boosting (xgboost v1.7.8.1)3 on R Studio. Data from the observations of 55,000 children’s attendances to Bristol’s Royal Hospital for Children ED were provided to the model. 80% of the sample was used for training and 20% for evaluation. Observation sets that did not have a heart rate or age recorded were excluded. We chose a pragmatic measure of ‘illness’: a total length of stay ≥ 24 hours and a C-reactive protein > 80 mg/L. Parameters used included: heart rate, respiratory rate, blood pressure, temperature, oxygen saturations, oxygen concentration of additional oxygen support, triage category code and capillary refill time. The training and testing stages were repeated 100 times to calculate a mean area under receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) with the associated sensitivity and specificities. Conventionally an AUC of 1.0 signifies a perfect test and an AUC of 0.5 shows a test to be no better than random.4 What did you find? Our machine learning models had AUCs ranging from 0.855-0.942, showing a high ability to suggest which children are unwell. These models outperformed the National PEWS 5 (AUC 0.555), the Scotland PEWS 6 (AUC 0.555) and the ED-PEWS7 (AUC 0.546). The most significant parameter used in our models was age in months, suggesting part of the benefit of electronically calculated PEWS is they don’t have to arbitrarily group children into different age groups to fit the paper sheet. What does it mean? We found machine learning could be used to predict which children are unwell in ED using only their vital observations and age more accurately than current methods. Considering that previous versions of PEWS use a variety of parameters, a benefit of the machine learning model is that each parameter is weighted given its importance to make a more accurate prediction. We plan to now validate this model with a further years’ worth of data and explore its sensitivity to different definitions of illness. References Can paediatric early warning scores (PEWS) be used to guide the need for hospital admission and predict significant illness in children presenting to the emergency department? title: An Explainable Hybrid Machine Learning Framework for Binary Classification of Global Tsunamigenic Earthquakes Using Seismic and Geophysical Parameters
abstract: ABSTRACT Rapid identification of earthquakes capable of generating tsunamis is a critical component of global tsunami hazard mitigation. In this study, we propose an explainable hybrid machine learning (ML) framework for the binary classification of tsunamigenic versus non‐tsunamigenic earthquakes using a global empirical dataset covering the period 2001–2022. The dataset contains 782 earthquake events with seismic, geophysical and intensity‐related parameters, including magnitude, focal depth, geographic location and intensity measures such as Community Decimal Intensity (CDI), and Modified Mercalli intensity (MMI). Four ML models were evaluated, including support vector machine (SVM), random forest (RF), Extreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost) and logistic regression (LR). Hyperparameter optimization was performed using the Optuna optimization framework, which efficiently explores the hyperparameter space using adaptive sampling strategies. Among the evaluated models, the hybrid SVM‐Optuna model achieved the best predictive performance, reaching a recall of 0.98 and an F 1‐score of 0.98, demonstrating strong capability in identifying tsunamigenic earthquakes while minimizing missed events. To enhance model transparency, two explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) methods were integrated: SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations) and LIME (local interpretable model‐agnostic explanations). These methods were used to interpret both global feature importance and local prediction behaviour. The explainability analysis revealed that shallow focal depth, earthquake magnitude and intensity‐related parameters are the most influential predictors of tsunami occurrence, which is consistent with established seismological understanding. It is important to emphasize that the proposed framework focuses on binary classification of tsunami occurrence at the earthquake source level. The model does not predict tsunami wave height, arrival time, inundation depth or coastal impact. Instead, it is designed as a rapid screening tool that can support the early stages of tsunami warning workflows.

To enhance model transparency, two explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) methods were integrated: SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations) and LIME (local interpretable model‐agnostic explanations). These methods were used to interpret both global feature importance and local prediction behaviour. The explainability analysis revealed that shallow focal depth, earthquake magnitude and intensity‐related parameters are the most influential predictors of tsunami occurrence, which is consistent with established seismological understanding. It is important to emphasize that the proposed framework focuses on binary classification of tsunami occurrence at the earthquake source level. The model does not predict tsunami wave height, arrival time, inundation depth or coastal impact. Instead, it is designed as a rapid screening tool that can support the early stages of tsunami warning workflows.

title: Radar signal modulation recognition via local-global feature focus with integrated AgentTrans module
abstract: To address the problem of decreased recognition accuracy caused by feature degradation and noise interference in low signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) environments, this paper proposes a recognition method that integrates multiple attention mechanisms. The proposed approach combines Convolutional Neural Networks, Residual Networks, and Transformer architectures to fully exploit their respective advantages in local feature extraction, deep semantic representation, and global modeling. The input to the model is a preprocessed time-frequency image of radar signals. Initially, spatial features are enhanced using convolutional layers and a DEConv-based upsampling module. Subsequently, multi-level features are extracted through the ELAB module and residual blocks. An AgentTrans module is then introduced, which effectively strengthens the modeling of key regional features by integrating multi-head attention with an agent-based selection mechanism. To further enhance the spatial contextual information, the model incorporates a Coordinate Attention mechanism. Finally, a Softmax classifier is employed to perform classification of 12 radar modulation signal types. Experiments conducted on a 12-class radar modulation dataset in standard TFRecord format demonstrate that the proposed method achieves a recognition accuracy of 94.67% under –10 dB SNR conditions, showing superior robustness and performance compared to existing approaches.

title: Lexical semantic change detection: A survey of tasks, benchmarks, models, and potential impacts in digital humanities and social sciences
abstract: Abstract Lexical semantic change (LSC) detection investigates changes in word meaning over time, focusing on language use at the lexical-semantic level from a diachronic perspective. The field has made significant progress over the past two decades, driven by the increased availability of multilingual benchmarks, notable performance improvements, and growing interdisciplinary applications. In this paper, we review the evolution of LSC models and benchmark constructions within the context of popular shared tasks. By categorizing LSC models into generations defined by key components, our investigation suggests that performance breakthroughs have been largely driven by advances in semantic representations , transitioning from count-based models to recent transformer-based approaches. Notably, transformer models have established themselves as state-of-the-art by integrating Word-in-Context tasks, which emphasize semantic proximity in context . Furthermore, we review substantial studies that primarily leverage diachronic word embeddings to explore political, social, and cultural contexts beyond the linguistic domain. Our work provides valuable insights for future model development and encourages further interdisciplinary exploration within digital humanities and social sciences.
